Greenhouse Effect. The warming mechanism by which atmospheric gases trap solar radiation, preventing heat from escaping to space. While a natural process essential for life, increasing concentrations of gases like carbon dioxide amplify the effect, leading to global warming and climate change.

Solar radiation passes through the atmosphere to warm Earth's surface. Earth re-emits this energy as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, nitrous oxide, ozone, and chlorofluorocarbons, are transparent to incoming visible light but strongly absorb outgoing infrared radiation. The absorbed heat is re-radiated in all directions, some escaping to space but much returning to the surface, causing net warming.

Without the natural greenhouse effect, maintained by water vapor, methane, and carbon dioxide at pre-industrial levels, Earth would be roughly sixty degrees Fahrenheit colder and largely uninhabitable. The effect became problematic only when human industrial activity intensified gas concentrations starting around eighteen hundred.

Fossil fuel combustion and deforestation release atmospheric carbon dioxide. Agriculture and industry release methane and nitrous oxide. The concentration of these greenhouse gases has risen dramatically since industrialization began. A doubling of atmospheric carbon dioxide is estimated to cause one-point-five to four-point-five degrees Celsius of warming, depending on climate feedback mechanisms. Water vapor, clouds, and ice albedo all play roles.

The greenhouse effect explains why the Moon, with no atmosphere, has temperature extremes. Earth maintains a stable, life-supporting climate until human-driven amplification destabilizes it. The atmosphere is the layer of gases trapping heat through the greenhouse effect. Meteorology is the science of weather and atmospheric processes including the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide is the primary human-contributed greenhouse gas. Climate is shaped and destabilized by greenhouse gas concentration changes. Radiation is the electromagnetic energy trapped by greenhouse gases, specifically infrared wavelengths.
